claim: Volume electron microscopy (EM) often requires weeks or months of continuous acquisition for large samples.
source: Volume electron microscopy (EM) is a time-consuming process – often requiring weeks or months of continuous acquisition for large samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Scheffer et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2018; Vergara et al., 2021) in the Introduction section.

claim: Targeting with an ultramicrotome is a difficult and manual process.
source: Targeting with an ultramicrotome is a difficult and manual process.
evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of ultramicrotome targeting, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Heavy metals make samples opaque, making it challenging to target regions deep within a sample.
source: This makes it challenging to target regions deep within a sample, especially when heavy metals make the sample opaque.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about how heavy metal staining affects sample visibility.

claim: The orientation of cutting must be set manually by adjusting three different ultramicrotome axes.
source: In addition, the orientation of cutting must be set manually by adjusting three different ultramicrotome axes.
evidence: This describes standard ultramicrotome operation based on established knowledge.

claim: X-ray is readily compatible with standard EM sample preparation methods.
source: X-ray offers many advantages for EM targeting – for example, it is readily compatible with standard EM sample preparation methods (Bosch et al., 2022; Kuan et al., 2020; Bushong et al., 2015; Karreman et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: X-ray provides images that highlight similar structures to volume EM, although at a lower resolution.
source: and provides images that highlight similar structures to volume EM (although at a lower resolution) (Bosch et al., 2022; Kuan et al., 2020; Bushong et al., 2015; Musser et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Laboratory micro-CT systems can provide an isotropic resolution of about 1 micron.
source: Laboratory micro-CT systems are becoming ever more popular and can provide an isotropic resolution of about 1 micron, with scan times in the range of a few hours (Withers et al., 2021; Karreman et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Synchrotrons can provide X-ray imaging resolutions in the range of hundreds or even tens of nanometres.
source: In addition, there is increasing access to synchrotrons for X-ray imaging, which can provide resolutions in the range of hundreds or even tens of nanometres, and scan times in the range of minutes (depending on the resolution required) (Withers et al., 2021; Bosch et al., 2022; Kuan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The motorised Leica system consists of three extra motors (one for each rotational axis) controlled by a Raspberry Pi computer.
source: For the UC7, this consisted of three extra motors (one for each rotational axis) controlled by a small Raspberry Pi computer (Figure 1B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description in the text and visual evidence in Figure 1B and D.

claim: The motorised RMC system has motors added to three rotational axes and two translational stage movements.
source: For the RMC, motors were added to the same rotational axes, with additional automation of the two translational stage movements (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description in the text and visual evidence in Figure 1C and E.

claim: Both ultramicrotome systems were calibrated with special adaptors that convert rotational movement into rotation of a Thorlabs CRM1PT/M rotation mount dial.
source: Both systems were calibrated with special adaptors made to convert a rotational movement into the rotation of the dial of a Thorlabs CRM1PT/M rotation mount, whose Vernier scale provides 5 arcmin (0.083°) resolution (see section 'Ultramicrotome systems and calibration).
evidence: The claim describes the calibration method used for the systems.

claim: The targeting problem was broken down into two steps: orientation and distance.
source: This targeting problem was broken down into two steps: orientation and distance.
evidence: This describes the approach taken in the study to solve the targeting problem.

claim: The orientation problem required finding a combination of three angles (knife tilt, sample tilt, sample rotation) that brought the target plane to be vertical and parallel to the knife.
source: For the orientation problem, we found a combination of three angles (knife tilt, sample tilt, sample rotation; Figure 1A) that brought the target plane to be vertical and parallel to the knife (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim describes the orientation solution approach and references figures showing the angles.

claim: The distance problem required finding the depth to cut from the sample surface to reach the target plane.
source: For the distance problem, we found the depth to cut from the sample surface to reach the target plane (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim describes the distance solution approach and references a figure.

claim: Forward and inverse kinematics equations were constructed for the ultramicrotome, similar to principles used in robotics.
source: We therefore applied similar principles, constructing a forward and inverse kinematics equation for the ultramicrotome.
evidence: The claim describes the mathematical approach used, drawing on robotics principles.

claim: Crosshair is an open-source Fiji plugin that allows user-friendly measurement of X-ray images and access to targeting calculations.
source: To make this workflow accessible to all, we developed the open-source Fiji (Schindelin et al., 2012) plugin Crosshair (https://github.com/automated-ultramicrotomy/crosshair; Meechan, 2022b), which allows user-friendly measurement of X-ray images, and access to the calculations described above (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim describes the software developed in this study, with reference to figures showing the interface.

claim: Crosshair uses BigDataViewer to allow browsing of large images in arbitrary 2D slices.
source: It uses BigDataViewer (Pietzsch et al., 2015) to allow browsing of large images in arbitrary 2D slices, and the ImageJ 3D Viewer (Schmid et al., 2010) to allow browsing in 3D.
evidence: The claim describes the software tools used in Crosshair, supported by citations.

claim: Crosshair has a 'microtome mode' which allows a simple representation of the ultramicrotome to be manipulated in 3D.
source: To make selection of solutions easier, Crosshair also has a 'microtome mode' which allows a simple representation of the ultramicrotome to be manipulated in 3D (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim describes a feature of the Crosshair software, with reference to a figure.

claim: Crosshair has a 'cutting mode' which allows the predicted cutting progression to be viewed in 2D and 3D.
source: Finally, Crosshair also has a 'cutting mode' which allows the predicted cutting progression to be viewed in 2D and 3D (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim describes a feature of the Crosshair software, with reference to a figure.

claim: Platynereis is a marine annelid that is an established model system for development, evolution, and neurobiology.

claim: Five samples were targeted with the motorised RMC system (samples f–j).
source: All samples were targeted with the workflow described above: five on the motorised Leica system (samples a–e) and five on the RMC system (samples f–j).

claim: All samples hit their target of cutting through both anterior dorsal cirrus.
source: Comparison of the target plane and trimmed block surface showed that all samples hit their target of cutting through both anterior dorsal cirrus, and provided similar Platynereis cross-sections to those predicted from the X-ray (Figure 7).

Samples a–e and f–j were targeted by different researchers, so this may also contribute to the differing average accuracy.

source: The workflow allows X-ray images of resin-embedded samples to be converted into a set of three angles (sample tilt, sample rotation, and knife tilt) and a cutting distance for the ultramicrotome.
evidence: This summarizes the main functionality of the workflow.

claim: Once X-ray images have been acquired, the Crosshair measurements and trimming can be done in 1–2 hours.
source: Once the X-ray images have been acquired, the Crosshair measurements and trimming can be done in 1–2 hr, depending on the sample.

claim: Non-assisted targeting from X-ray may take 1–2 days for complex samples.
source: This is a significant speed up where, in our experience, non-assisted targeting from X-ray may take 1–2 days for complex samples.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experience with traditional targeting methods.

claim: The resolution of X-ray images limits the achievable accuracy of the targeting system.
source: There are a number of factors that limit the accuracy of the current system – the first is the resolution of the X-ray images. All X-ray imaging in this article was done with lab-based micro-CT systems, which offer a maximum resolution of around 1 micron isotropic voxel size. As all measurements are based on these images, this voxel size limits the achievable accuracy and contributes to our registration uncertainty.
evidence: This is inference about factors limiting accuracy based on the experimental setup.

claim: Combining Crosshair with higher-resolution X-ray imaging from a synchrotron could improve accuracy.
source: A future direction would be to combine Crosshair with higher-resolution X-ray imaging from a synchrotron.
evidence: This is speculation about future improvements to the system.

claim: Manual steps in the targeting workflow introduce variation due to human error.
source: Another accuracy limitation are the manual steps that remain in this targeting workflow. While we automate the motorised movements and angle/distance calculations, a number of steps still require manual use of the ultramicrotome, and will therefore vary in accuracy depending on how experienced the user is.
evidence: This is inference about factors limiting accuracy.

claim: Each manual step should be minimised or eliminated in future work to improve accuracy.

claim: Automation of the knife approach step is challenging and would require hardware improvements.
source: Automation of this step is challenging and would require hardware improvements that extend the feed length of the ultramicrotome to minimise resets or a method to allow automatic resets.

claim: Crosshair's calculations should be applicable to any 3D map, not only X-ray.

source: In summary, this targeting workflow offers a first step towards fully automated targeting of structures within resin blocks for EM.

claim: Both ultramicrotome systems were calibrated using a Thorlabs CRM1PT/M rotation mount with 5 arcmin (0.083°) resolution.
source: In order to calibrate the number of degrees rotated by these stepper motors via different gear sets (not only gear sets for retrofitted motors but also internal gears in the original RMC and Leica sample holder and knife holder to conduct the rotation), therefore, different gear ratios, we designed special adaptors to convert the rotational movement of the sample holder and the knife holder to the rotation of the dial of a Thorlabs CRM1PT/M rotation mount, whose Vernier scale provides 5 arcmin (0.083°) resolution.

claim: A linear regression was performed to work out the microstep numbers of the angle resolution.

evidence: This is inference about the limitations of the measurement accuracy.

claim: Measurement precision could be improved in future by moving to higher-resolution X-ray imaging from synchrotrons.
source: This could be improved in future by moving to higher-resolution X-ray imaging from synchrotrons, which can provide resolutions in the range of hundreds of nanometres.
evidence: This is speculation about future improvements.

claim: Samples a–e were X-ray imaged with a different micro-CT system than samples f–j.

evidence: This describes a difference in the experimental setup between sample groups.

claim: Non-assisted targeting from X-ray is a slower process than the Crosshair workflow.

claim: Synchrotrons offer faster scan times than lab-based micro-CT systems.
source: In addition, there is increasing access to synchrotrons for X-ray imaging, which can provide resolutions in the range of hundreds or even tens of nanometres, and scan times in the range of minutes (depending on the resolution required) (Withers et al., 2021; Bosch et al., 2022; Kuan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The combination of X-ray imaging from synchrotrons with EM is becoming more popular.
source: In recent years, there have been a number of studies that combine X-ray imaging from a synchrotron with EM (Bosch et al., 2022; Kuan et al., 2020; Musser et al., 2021), demonstrating the power of combining the large field of view and fast scan times of X-ray, with the high resolution of targeted EM acquisition. As this combination becomes ever more popular, it is more important than ever to have user-friendly targeting solutions like Crosshair.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies and inference about the trend.

source: A positive error indicates that the sample was trimmed too far, while a negative error indicates it was not trimmed enough.
